sections.title: ① Concept Explanation
sections.body: An **AI Agent** is an autonomous software system that perceives its environment, reasons about goals, selects actions (including tool calls), executes them, and iterates until a goal is achieved — without requiring step-by-step human instruction. Unlike a simple LLM call (stateless, single-turn), an agent maintains **state**, manages **memory**, uses **tools**, and runs in a **loop**. The anatomy of an agent consists of five core components: a **Brain** (the LLM), **Memory** (context/stores), **Tools** (external capabilities), a **Planner** (decomposition logic), and an **Executor** (action runner). Agents matter because they enable LLMs to solve multi-step, real-world tasks that require external data, computation, and decision-making. In production systems, agents are the fundamental building block of systems like autonomous coding assistants, research pipelines, customer service orchestration, and financial analysis bots.

diagrams.title: Anatomy of an agent: model + tools + memory + loop
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  U(["User goal"]) --> L
  subgraph A["Agent"]
    L["LLM brain - decides next step"]
    M[("Memory - history, facts")]
    P["Planner - break goal into steps"]
    L <--> M
    L <--> P
  end
  L -- "tool call" --> T["Tools - APIs, DB, search, code"]
  T -- "observation" --> L
  L -- "final answer" --> R(["Response"])
diagrams.explain: A chatbot is only the **LLM box**: text in, text out. An **agent** wraps the LLM in a loop and gives it **tools** (to act on the world), **memory** (to remember across steps and turns) and optionally a **planner**. The arrows between LLM and tools repeat until the LLM decides it has enough information to answer — that repetition is what makes it an agent.

quiz.question: What are the five anatomical components of an AI agent and how do they interact?
options: deterministic agent** follows fixed control flow — the same input always produces the same sequence of actions (e.g., rule-based workflow).
The scratchpad is the accumulated Thought+Action+Observation history within a single agent run.
A thick agent encodes business logic in code (pre/post processing, routing rules) and uses the LLM only where judgment is genuinely needed — more predictable and cheaper.
Interaction flow: The LLM receives the goal + memory context → reasons → generates a tool call or final answer → executor runs the tool → result is appended to memory → LLM reasons again…
quiz.explanation: The five components are: Brain (LLM) — Reasons, generates plans, decides next actions Memory — Stores context (short-term: conversation history; long-term: vector DB) Tools — External APIs, search, calculators, code interpreters Planner — Decomposes goals into subtasks, manages execution order Executor — Runs tool calls, handles responses, feeds back into the loop Interaction flow: The LLM receives the goal + memory…

quiz.question: How does an AI agent differ from a simple LLM completion call?
options: OpenAI's function calling is a structured version of ReAct where: Thought = The LLM's internal reasoning (hidden, not shown in message); Action = tool_calls field in the response (structured JSON, not free-text); Observation = The role: "tool" message added to conversation.

Choose workflow automation when: Tasks are fully predictable and well-defined (same steps every time); Reliability is paramount (no tolerance for LLM hallucination); Latency is critical (no LLM inference overhead).

Follow this 6-step design process: Define the goal space — What tasks will this agent solve? What's out of scope?; Identify required tools — What external capabilities are needed (search, DB, APIs)?; Design the memory architecture — Short-term (context window), long-term (vector store)?.
stateless** — it takes input, returns output, and forgets everything.
quiz.explanation: stateless** — it takes input, returns output, and forgets everything. An agent is stateful and iterative: it maintains memory across turns, uses tools to gather real-world data, and runs a loop until the goal is met. Agents can call APIs, search databases, execute code, and make sequential decisions — tasks impossible with one-shot completions. ---

quiz.question: What is the role of the system prompt in agent anatomy?
options: Autonomy — Agents act without per-step human instruction; chatbots respond to every message; Tool Use — Agents call external APIs and tools; chatbots only generate text; Goal Persistence — Agents maintain a goal across multiple steps; chatbots answer one message at a time.
deterministic agent** follows fixed control flow — the same input always produces the same sequence of actions (e.g., rule-based workflow).
A thick agent encodes business logic in code (pre/post processing, routing rules) and uses the LLM only where judgment is genuinely needed — more predictable and cheaper.
The system prompt is the agent's constitution — it defines identity, capabilities, constraints, output format, and behavioral guardrails.
quiz.explanation: The system prompt is the agent's constitution — it defines identity, capabilities, constraints, output format, and behavioral guardrails. In a multi-step loop, the system prompt persists across all iterations as the first message. Production agents include: role definition, tool usage instructions, output format spec, safety guardrails, and escalation rules. ---

quiz.question: How does agent state differ from agent memory?
options: Measure: Task completion rate — % of tasks completed end-to-end without human intervention; Time savings — Average human time replaced per task; Error rate — Agent errors vs. human errors on same tasks.
Silent failure occurs when: (1) a tool returns an empty string or None and the agent treats it as valid data, (2) the LLM generates a plausible-sounding but incorrect…

Termination conditions prevent infinite loops: Max iterations — Hard cap on loop count; Confidence threshold — Agent signals sufficient confidence in answer; Goal achievement signal — LLM explicitly outputs FINAL_ANSWER.
State is the live, mutable snapshot of the agent's current execution context — what step it's on, what variables are set, what tools have been called.
quiz.explanation: State is the live, mutable snapshot of the agent's current execution context — what step it's on, what variables are set, what tools have been called. Memory is the persistent store of information the agent has accumulated — conversation history, retrieved documents, past decisions. State is ephemeral (lost when the loop ends); memory can be persisted (to disk, vector DB, Redis).

quiz.question: What causes an agent to fail silently vs. raise an exception?
options: Termination conditions prevent infinite loops: Max iterations — Hard cap on loop count; Confidence threshold — Agent signals sufficient confidence in answer; Goal achievement signal — LLM explicitly outputs FINAL_ANSWER.

Measure: Task completion rate — % of tasks completed end-to-end without human intervention; Time savings — Average human time replaced per task; Error rate — Agent errors vs. human errors on same tasks.

Separate evaluation: Reasoning quality: Does the Thought correctly identify what's needed? (Human review or LLM-as-judge); Action selection: Does the agent pick the right tool and arguments? (Compare against golden dataset); Observation utilization: Does the agent correctly use the observation to update its next thought?.
Silent failure occurs when: (1) a tool returns an empty string or None and the agent treats it as valid data, (2) the LLM generates a plausible-sounding but incorrect…
quiz.explanation: Silent failure occurs when: (1) a tool returns an empty string or None and the agent treats it as valid data, (2) the LLM generates a plausible-sounding but incorrect continuation, (3) there's no output validation layer. This is the most dangerous production failure mode.
